analogy.p: A **mixture** is like a fruit salad: apple, grape and banana pieces are just placed together, you can pick them out, and each still tastes of itself. A **compound** is like a baked cake: eggs, flour and sugar have been chemically changed into something new, with new properties, and you cannot pick the eggs back out. The comparison breaks down because a cake can contain any recipe amount while a true compound always has fixed atom ratios (water is always H₂O), and real recipes do not rearrange atoms.

bullets: The symbol is **one capital letter**, or **a capital followed by a small letter**: O is oxygen, Na is sodium, Cl is chlorine. Writing 'CO' (carbon monoxide) versus 'Co' (cobalt) shows why the capital letters matter.

Some symbols come from old Latin names: Na (natrium) for sodium, K (kalium) for potassium, Fe (ferrum) for iron, Cu (cuprum) for copper, Pb (plumbum) for lead, Ag (argentum) for silver, Au (aurum) for gold.

You must know the **names and symbols of the first 20 elements** (H to Ca), the elements of **Group 1 and Group 7**, and other common ones in the specification such as Fe, Cu, Zn, Ag, Au, Pb, Al and Mg.
A symbol on its own (e.g. Fe) stands for **one atom** of the element. The same symbol with a number in front (e.g. 3Fe) means three separate atoms.
An atom of one element is different from an atom of another element because it has a different number of protons (the atomic number), which is covered in the atomic structure topics.
Link: atoms are much too small to see. Your knowledge of them comes from **models** and evidence, which is why the model of the atom has changed over time.
core.p: Everything is made of **atoms**. An atom is the smallest part of an element that can still be called that element, and atoms are extremely small, with a radius of about **0.1 nm (1 × 10⁻¹⁰ m)**. Each element has its own **chemical symbol**, a one or two letter code that stands for one atom of that element. Using symbols means scientists everywhere can write the same short code regardless of language.

bullets: Every atom in a sample of an element is the same type, so a sample of pure iron contains only Fe atoms and a sample of pure oxygen gas contains only oxygen atoms.

Elements can exist as **single atoms** (the noble gases such as He, Ne and Ar), as **molecules of the same atoms** (O₂, N₂, H₂, Cl₂, Br₂, I₂ are all diatomic, meaning two atoms joined), or as **giant structures** (metals, diamond, graphite).
The periodic table lists the elements in order of **atomic number**; its layout groups elements with similar properties in vertical columns (groups).
Elements are broadly split into **metals** and **non-metals**; this is dealt with in later periodic table topics.
An element like O₂ is still an **element**, even though its particles are molecules, because the molecule contains only one type of atom. This is a very common exam trap.
Ozone (O₃) and oxygen (O₂) are both elements made of oxygen atoms only, but they are different substances with different properties.
core.p: An **element** is a substance made of only one type of atom. There are about **100 different elements**, and they are all arranged in the **periodic table**. Elements cannot be broken down into anything simpler by chemical reactions, because there is nothing simpler to break them into. Everything around you, including living things, is built from combinations of these elements.

bullets: The two main types of bonding that hold compounds together are **ionic bonding** (metal + non-metal, transfer of electrons) and **covalent bonding** (non-metals, shared electrons). These are covered in the bonding topics.

**Fixed proportions** means the ratio of atoms is always the same: water is always H₂O (two hydrogen atoms to one oxygen atom), carbon dioxide is always CO₂. If the ratio is different it is a different compound (CO is carbon monoxide).
Compounds can only be separated into their elements by **chemical reactions** (such as electrolysis or thermal decomposition), not by physical methods like filtering or evaporating.

The **name** often tells you the elements: sodium chloride contains sodium and chlorine; names ending **-ide** (chloride, oxide, sulfide) show a compound of just two elements; names ending **-ate** (sulfate, nitrate, carbonate) show oxygen is also present.
Because a compound is a single substance, it has its own fixed properties such as melting point and boiling point.

Link: Compounds are named from formulae or symbol equations. Examples to know: NaCl sodium chloride, MgO magnesium oxide, CO₂ carbon dioxide, H₂O water, NH₃ ammonia, CH₄ methane, HCl hydrogen chloride, CaCO₃ calcium carbonate.
core.p: A **compound** is a substance made of two or more different elements **chemically combined** (joined by chemical bonds) in **fixed proportions**. Compounds are formed from elements by **chemical reactions**. The compound usually has completely different properties from the elements that made it, because the atoms have been rearranged into a new substance. For example, sodium is a soft, reactive metal and chlorine is a poisonous gas, yet sodium chloride is the harmless white solid in table salt.

bullets: Signs of a chemical reaction include a **colour change**, **gas given off** (bubbles), **a precipitate forming**, and a **temperature change**; none of these alone is proof, but new substance formation is the definition.
Energy changes are detectable as a rise in temperature (exothermic) or a fall in temperature (endothermic) of the surroundings.
Atoms are **not created or destroyed** in a reaction, they are only rearranged, so the total mass of reactants equals the total mass of products (conservation of mass).
Reactions can be shown by a **word equation** (e.g. iron + sulfur → iron sulfide) or a **symbol equation** (Fe + S → FeS).
The arrow in the equation means 'reacts to make'. Reactants are on the left, products are on the right.
Ordinary melting, freezing, boiling, condensing and dissolving are **physical changes** because no new substance is made.
core.p: A **chemical reaction** always involves the formation of **one or more new substances**, and it often involves a **detectable energy change**. This is the key difference between a chemical change and a physical change such as melting or dissolving. In a physical change the substance is the same before and after; in a chemical change atoms are rearranged to make different substances.

bullets: H₂O: 2 hydrogen atoms and 1 oxygen atom, so 3 atoms in total from 2 different elements.
Ca(OH)₂: 1 Ca, then (OH) twice, so 2 O and 2 H, giving 5 atoms in total.
Al₂(SO₄)₃: 2 Al, and (SO₄) three times gives 3 S and 3 × 4 = 12 O, so 17 atoms in total.
A big number **in front** of a formula (a coefficient, e.g. 2H₂O) multiplies the **whole** formula: 2H₂O is 4 H atoms and 2 O atoms.
Never change a subscript to balance an equation, because that changes the substance; only change the number in front.
The formula of an **element** that is a molecule, such as O₂ or Cl₂, uses a subscript to show atoms joined together but is still an element.
Link: you may be asked to **name** compounds from formulae, e.g. Na₂SO₄ is sodium sulfate, Mg(OH)₂ is magnesium hydroxide.
core.p: A **formula** uses chemical symbols and numbers to show which elements are in a compound and the ratio of their atoms. The small number written below and after a symbol is the **subscript**, and it tells you how many atoms of **that element** are present. If there is no number, there is **one** atom. Brackets are used when a group of atoms is repeated, and the number after the bracket multiplies everything inside.

bullets: Word equation: magnesium + oxygen → magnesium oxide.
Symbol equation: 2Mg + O₂ → 2MgO. Check: left has 2 Mg and 2 O; right has 2 Mg and 2 O. Balanced.
Iron and sulfur: Fe + S → FeS is already balanced (1 Fe, 1 S each side).
Hydrogen and oxygen: 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O. Left: 4 H, 2 O; right: 4 H, 2 O.
**State symbols** can be added: (s) solid, (l) liquid, (g) gas, (aq) aqueous, meaning dissolved in water.
Higher tier link: you may need to write balanced half equations and ionic equations later in the course.
core.p: Chemical reactions can be represented by **word equations** or **symbol equations**. A word equation gives the names of the reactants and products. A symbol equation uses formulae and must be **balanced**, which means the same number of each type of atom is on both sides, because atoms cannot be created or destroyed. Balancing is done by putting numbers in front of the formulae, never by altering the formulae.

bullets: Air is a mixture of nitrogen, oxygen, argon, carbon dioxide and other gases (about 78% nitrogen and 21% oxygen) in changeable proportions.
Seawater is a mixture of water, dissolved salts and other substances.
Alloys such as brass or steel are mixtures of metals (and sometimes carbon); crude oil is a mixture of hydrocarbons.
Mixtures do not have a fixed melting or boiling point; they melt or boil over a **range of temperatures**.
Mixtures can be separated by **physical processes** because the substances are not bonded.
A mixture can contain elements, compounds, or both.
core.p: A **mixture** consists of **two or more elements or compounds not chemically combined together**. The substances are simply mixed, with no chemical bonds formed between them. Because of this, the **chemical properties of each substance in the mixture are unchanged**. The mixture can contain any proportions of the substances; there is no fixed ratio, unlike a compound.

bullets: Filtration separates an **insoluble solid** from a liquid because the solid particles are too big to pass through the filter paper.
Crystallisation and simple distillation separate a **soluble solid** from its solvent.
Fractional distillation separates a mixture of **liquids** with different boiling points.
Chromatography separates substances by how soluble they are in the solvent and how strongly they stick to the paper.
Detail on each technique and the apparatus is in the 'Separation techniques' notes.
Contrast: separating a compound into elements needs a **chemical** reaction, e.g. electrolysis.
core.h: 8. Physical separation: no chemical reaction, no new substance
core.p: The physical processes that separate mixtures are **filtration, crystallisation, simple distillation, fractional distillation and chromatography**. These **do not involve chemical reactions and no new substances are made**. They rely on a difference in a **physical property** such as solubility, particle size, boiling point or how strongly substances stick to a surface. The substances you collect at the end are the same ones that you started with.

bullets: Mixture: iron and sulfur can be present in **any proportion**; compound: Fe and S atoms in a **1 : 1** ratio in FeS.
Mixture: separated by a magnet (physical); compound: cannot be separated by a magnet, only by a chemical reaction.
Mixture: iron and sulfur each keep their **own properties**; compound: shows **different properties** from either element.
Making the compound needs an energy input to start, and the reaction then gives out heat energy.
Equation: Fe + S → FeS (iron + sulfur → iron sulfide).
Exam use: this is the standard example for '**explain the difference between a mixture and a compound**'.
core.h: 9. Iron and sulfur: the classic comparison
core.p: Mixing iron filings and sulfur powder gives a **mixture**: the yellow and grey particles can still be seen, a **magnet** pulls out the iron, and each substance keeps its own properties. If the mixture is **heated**, the elements react to form the compound **iron sulfide, FeS**: a dark grey solid that is **not magnetic** and has new properties. The compound is now a single substance and a magnet no longer separates anything.

bullets: **Bonding:** compound atoms are chemically bonded; mixture substances are not.
**Proportions:** compound has fixed ratio (H₂O is always 2:1); mixture can vary.
**Properties:** compound has new properties different from its elements; mixture components keep their own properties.
**Separation:** compound needs a chemical reaction; mixture needs physical processes.
**Energy:** forming a compound usually has a detectable energy change; mixing usually does not.
**Melting/boiling:** a compound has fixed melting and boiling points; a mixture melts or boils over a range.
**Formula:** compound has a formula; a mixture does not.
core.p: Examiners regularly ask you to compare these two. The central ideas are **chemical combination, fixed proportions, properties and separation method**. The best answers use all four, and refer to a named example. Remember that a compound is a **single pure substance**, whereas a mixture contains **several substances**.

bullets: Melting point and boiling point data can be used to **distinguish pure substances from mixtures**.
A pure substance gives **one spot** in chromatography; a mixture gives more than one.
A sharp melting point (e.g. 80 °C exactly) suggests purity; a melting range suggests a mixture.
Pure substances are important in medicines and food, where contamination must be avoided.
Formulations such as fuels, alloys, paints and fertilisers are designed mixtures made to have useful properties.
core.p: In chemistry, a **pure substance** is a **single element or compound, not mixed with any other substance**. This is stricter than everyday use: orange juice 'pure and natural' is chemically a mixture. A pure element or compound melts and boils at **specific temperatures**, for example pure water freezes at 0 °C and boils at 100 °C at normal pressure. Impurities lower the melting point and spread it over a range, and raise the boiling point.

bullets: Link to **conservation of mass**: the total mass stays the same because atoms are only rearranged.
Link to **empirical formula**: the simplest whole-number ratio of atoms in a compound shows the fixed proportions.
Link to **electrolysis**: a chemical method that splits compounds into elements.
Link to **atmosphere**: air is a mixture, and its components can be separated by physical methods.
Link to **periodic table**: elements with similar properties form similar compounds.
core.p: At Higher tier the same ideas are used for harder tasks: balancing more complex symbol equations, deducing formulae from data, and explaining why the properties of a compound differ from its elements. The key reasoning is that **properties depend on the bonding and structure**, not on the elements alone. When atoms form a compound their outer electrons are transferred or shared, creating a completely new structure.

exam: Command word **'State'/'Name'** (1 mark): one word or short answer, e.g. 'compound' for H₂O.

**'Describe the difference between a compound and a mixture' (2 marks):** one mark for 'compound: elements chemically combined' and one for 'mixture: not chemically combined'. Add 'fixed proportions' and 'separated physically' for extra detail in 3-4 mark versions.

**Iron and sulfur (4 marks):** say the mixture can be separated with a **magnet**, iron and sulfur **keep their properties**; heating makes **iron sulfide**, a **new substance** that is **not magnetic** and has **different properties**; its atoms are **chemically bonded**.
**Classification questions:** decide if one type of atom (element), fixed ratio bonded (compound), or several substances (mixture). Give a reason, not just a label.
**Atom counting (1 to 3 marks):** write the numbers for each element separately, then add them for the total. Show working.
**Balancing equations (2 marks):** one mark for correct formulae, one for the correct balancing numbers. Check that atoms match on both sides.
**'Explain why' questions (2-3 marks):** link a cause to an effect: 'because the atoms are chemically bonded, so the compound has different properties'.
**Naming compounds:** -ide means two elements; -ate means oxygen is present as well.
**Particle diagrams:** a compound shows touching different atoms in the same pattern; a mixture shows separate particles; an element shows all the same atoms.
Use **precise words**: 'chemically combined', 'fixed proportions', 'physical process', 'no new substance'.
**Use an example** (iron sulfide, water, air) whenever the question lets you; examiners reward it.

mistakes.r: Elements in a compound are **chemically combined** (bonded), not just mixed.
It is an **element**: both atoms are the same type.
mistakes.w: Saying O₂ or N₂ is a compound because it has two atoms.

mistakes.r: In a mixture the **chemical properties of each substance are unchanged**; no reaction happens.
mistakes.w: Saying mixtures have no properties of their own or that the substances 'react'.

mistakes.r: Water is a **compound** with fixed H₂O ratio; hydrogen and oxygen are chemically combined.
mistakes.w: Saying 'water is a mixture of hydrogen and oxygen'.

mistakes.r: Only change the **number in front** of a formula; subscripts define the substance.
mistakes.w: Changing the small numbers in a formula to balance an equation.

mistakes.r: Compounds can only be separated into elements by **chemical reactions**.
mistakes.w: Saying a compound can be separated by filtering or evaporating.

mistakes.r: Capital first, small second: Cl, Co, Na.
mistakes.w: Writing symbols with the wrong case, e.g. CL, co, NA.

mistakes.r: A pure substance is a single element or compound; these are **mixtures**.
Multiply everything in the bracket: Ca(OH)₂ has 1 Ca, 2 O, 2 H.
mistakes.w: Counting only the first atom in Ca(OH)₂ or ignoring the bracket multiplier.

summary: AQA wants you to know that atoms are represented by chemical symbols, that about 100 elements are shown in the periodic table, that compounds are made from elements by chemical reactions and have fixed proportions and formulae, and that mixtures are not chemically combined so each substance keeps its own properties. This is the foundation for every other chemistry topic: you must be able to classify a substance, read a formula, and say how a compound differs from a mixture.

terms.d: The smallest part of an element that can exist; very small, with a radius of about 0.1 nm.
A substance made of only one type of atom; about 100 are known and shown in the periodic table.
One or two letters used to represent an atom of an element, e.g. O, Na.
A substance of two or more elements chemically combined in fixed proportions.
Shows the symbols and the ratio of atoms of each element in a compound.
Two or more elements or compounds not chemically combined together.
A change in which one or more new substances are formed, often with a detectable energy change.
A single element or compound, not mixed with any other substance.
A method of separation that involves no chemical reaction and makes no new substances.
A way to represent a reaction using the names of the reactants and products.
A way to represent a reaction using formulae; must be balanced.
The small number in a formula that gives the number of atoms of the preceding element.
A molecule made of two atoms joined, e.g. O₂, H₂, Cl₂.
A substance that is used up in a chemical reaction.
A substance made in a chemical reaction.

worked.ans: In the mixture the iron and sulfur are not chemically combined so the iron can be removed with a magnet and each keeps its own properties. When heated they react to form iron sulfide (Fe + S → FeS), a compound in which the iron and sulfur atoms are chemically bonded in a fixed ratio. Iron sulfide is not magnetic and has different properties from both elements, and it can only be split up by a chemical reaction.
worked.q: Iron filings and sulfur powder are mixed together. The mixture is then heated and iron sulfide forms. Compare the mixture with iron sulfide. (4 marks)
steps: Identify what the mixture is: iron and sulfur are not chemically combined.
State how the mixture behaves: a magnet pulls out the iron so physical separation is possible; each element keeps its own properties.
State what happens on heating: a chemical reaction makes a new substance, iron sulfide, FeS.
Compare properties: iron sulfide is not magnetic and has different properties; the atoms are chemically bonded in a fixed 1:1 ratio.

worked.q: Calculate the total number of atoms in one formula unit of aluminium sulfate, Al₂(SO₄)₃. (3 marks)
steps: Al: the subscript 2 gives 2 aluminium atoms.
Bracket (SO₄) is multiplied by 3: S = 1 × 3 = 3 and O = 4 × 3 = 12.

worked.ans: Elements: oxygen, ozone. Compound: ammonia. Mixtures: seawater, brass. Reason example: ammonia is a compound because nitrogen and hydrogen atoms are chemically bonded in a fixed ratio of 1 N to 3 H.
worked.q: The table lists substances: oxygen (O₂), seawater, ammonia (NH₃), brass, ozone (O₃). Classify each as element, compound or mixture and give a reason for one. (3 marks)
steps: O₂ and O₃: only oxygen atoms, so elements.
NH₃: nitrogen and hydrogen chemically combined in a 1:3 ratio, so a compound.
Seawater and brass: several substances not chemically combined, so mixtures.
